paper.title: ELEVATE-LNP: Empty lipid nanoparticle enabled validation and AI-guided therapeutic evaluation for efficient formulation optimization for mRNA delivery

scope.included: All nonempty rows and columns of si2.xlsx and si3.xlsx; all six formulation rows in Word Table S1; shared methods; registered experimental figure endpoints.
scope.excluded: Numerical extraction of ML benchmarking, SHAP, correlations, virtual landscapes, references and author metadata. Image-derived individual results remain pending.
scope.cross_file_identity: IDs are source-local; no cross-file merging on sample number.
scope.review_protocol: Review values, units, method applicability and scoped completeness. accept/correct/reject/unresolved. Excel edits do not automatically modify JSON.

ELEVATE-LNP: Empty lipid nanoparticle enabled validation and AI-guided 
therapeutic evaluation for efficient formulation optimization for 
mRNA delivery

Mingzhi Yu a,1, Luhan Wang a,1, Timothy Elliott a, Xianqing Wang b, Allen Mathew a, Bei Qiu b,  
Liang Yao b, Wenxin Wang b, Nan Zhang a,*

a Centre of Micro/Nano Manufacturing Technology (MNMT-Dublin), School of Mechanical & Materials Engineering, University College Dublin, D04 V1W8, Ireland
b Charles Institute of Dermatology, School of Medicine, University College Dublin, D04 V1W8, Dublin, Ireland
A R T I C L E  I N F O

Keywords:
Lipid nanoparticles
Microfluidics
Machine learning
mRNA delivery
High-throughput optimization
A B S T R A C T

Lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) have emerged as a leading platform for mRNA delivery, particularly following the 
success of SARS-CoV-2 mRNA vaccines. However, identifying effective LNP formulations remains time- 
consuming because of the large and complex multicomponent formulation space. Here, we present ELEVATE- 
LNP an Empty-LNP-Enabled Validation and AI-Guided Therapeutic Evaluation platform by integrating a high- 
throughput parallelized microfluidic preparation with physicochemical characterization and machine learning 
for mid-stream and downstream LNP formulation optimization when ionizable lipids are shortlisted. A broad 
formulation space comprising four ionizable lipids, different helper lipids, lipid ratios, and process conditions 
was first screened using empty LNPs to identify formulations with desirable particle size and polydispersity index 
(PDI). Machine-learning analysis was then used to determine the formulation and process parameters associated 
with empty-LNP properties. Selected candidates were subsequently evaluated following mRNA encapsulation by 
assessing particle size, PDI, encapsulation efficiency, cell viability, and transfection performance. The results 
revealed lipid-dependent relationships between formulation parameters and the physicochemical properties of 
empty LNPs. Six features were strongly associated with particle size, while eleven features contributed to vari­
ations in PDI. GFP expression in CFBE cells demonstrated that SM-102-based LNPs achieved higher transfection 
efficiency than CKK-E12-based formulations. In a separate CFTR mRNA evaluation, DOPC-containing LNPs 
produced higher CFTR protein expression than their DSPC-containing counterparts. By integrating empty-LNP 
prescreening with subsequent payload-based validation, the ELEVATE-LNP workflow reduces the number of 
candidates and the amount of nucleic acid required for functional testing. The platform therefore provides a 
practical approach for narrowing lipid-ratio and formulation-condition spaces within preselected ionizable lipid 
systems.

Cystic fibrosis (CF) is a life-limiting genetic disorder caused by mu­
tations in the cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator 
(CFTR) gene, leading to impaired ion transport, mucus accumulation, 
and progressive lung dysfunction [1–5]. Although small-molecule 
modulators have improved clinical outcomes for subsets of patients, a 
significant proportion of CF mutations remain unaddressed [6–8]. In this 
context, messenger RNA (mRNA)–based therapeutics have emerged as a

promising strategy to restore functional CFTR protein expression in a 
mutation-agnostic manner [9]. However, the intrinsic instability of 
mRNA and its limited ability to cross biological barriers necessitate the 
development of efficient delivery systems [10,11]. Although mRNA- 
mediated protein restoration is transient, repeated administration can 
sustain therapeutic CFTR levels over time, as supported by early clinical 
studies such as MRT5005, highlighting the potential of mRNA delivery 
as a viable treatment modality for CF. [12,13]
Lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) have become the leading platform for

E-mail address: nan.zhang@ucd.ie (N. Zhang). 
1 These authors contributed equally: Mingzhi Yu, Luhan Wang.

https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cej.2026.180282

Available online 3 August 2026 
1385-8947/© 2026 The Authors. Published by Elsevier B.V. This is an open access article under the CC BY license ( http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ ).

mRNA delivery, owing to their ability to encapsulate nucleic acids, 
protect them from degradation, and facilitate intracellular delivery 
[14–19]. In recent years, substantial efforts have been devoted to the 
development of novel ionizable lipids to enhance delivery efficiency and 
biocompatibility [20–22]. Despite these advances, the design of LNP 
formulations remains largely empirical. LNP performance is governed 
by a complex interplay of formulation parameters, including ionizable 
lipids, helper lipids, cholesterol, and PEG-lipids, which collectively in­
fluence nanoparticle size, stability, and biological activity [23–28]. The 
high dimensionality of this formulation space, coupled with nonlinear 
interactions between components, makes rational optimization chal­
lenging and often reliant on trial-and-error approaches [29].

Microfluidic technologies have been widely adopted to improve the 
reproducibility and control of LNP synthesis, enabling precise manipu­
lation of mixing conditions and particle formation [30,31]. Neverthe­
less, conventional microfluidic platforms are typically limited in 
throughput, restricting their ability to efficiently explore large formu­
lation spaces. In parallel, machine learning approaches have been 
introduced to accelerate LNP design by modeling relationships between 
formulation parameters and physicochemical properties [32]. Recent 
studies have further demonstrated the potential of deep learning, mo­
lecular descriptors, foundation models, and multi-objective AI strategies 
to accelerate ionizable lipid discovery and improve LNP engineering for 
mRNA delivery [33–35]. For example, the AGILE platform integrates 
deep learning with combinatorial chemistry for rapid ionizable lipid 
development [33]. These studies highlight the importance of incorpo­
rating lipid structural information and molecular-level descriptors into 
predictive models. However, many formulation studies still rely pri­
marily on categorical lipid identity or bulk formulation variables, and 
the integration of high-throughput formulation-level datasets with 
payload-specific biological evaluation remains limited. Furthermore, 
the lack of high-quality, experimentally consistent datasets continues to 
constrain the robustness and generalizability of ML models for LNP 
formulation design.

A critical but underexplored challenge lies in bridging early physi­
cochemical optimization with payload-specific functional evaluation. 
Direct screening of mRNA-loaded LNPs is costly and labor-intensive

because it requires nucleic acid payloads, encapsulation measure­
ments, and cell-based assays. Empty LNPs provide a more efficient route 
for early-stage screening by identifying formulations with suitable size 
and polydispersity index (PDI). Because mRNA loading can increase 
particle size, selecting smaller empty LNPs may help mRNA-loaded 
particles remain within the commonly used sub-150 nm range for 
cellular delivery. Therefore, empty LNPs should be used as an upstream 
filtering step rather than a direct substitute for mRNA-loaded 
characterization.

To address these challenges, we developed ELEVATE-LNP (Empty- 
LNP Enabled Validation and AI-guided Therapeutic Evaluation), an in­
tegrated 
microfluidics–machine 
learning 
framework 
for 
high- 
throughput formulation optimization and biological validation, as 
illustrated in Fig. 1. The framework follows a stage-gated strategy to 
screen broadly, learn efficiently, and validate therapeutically. First, 
ELEVATE-LNP screens broadly by exploring a large formulation space of 
empty LNPs using parallelized microfluidic synthesis with MiNANO- 
form [36] and high-throughput DLS characterization. It then learns 
efficiently through machine learning–based analysis and down-selection 
of candidates with desirable physicochemical properties. Selected for­
mulations are subsequently evaluated after GFP mRNA encapsulation in 
CF-relevant cellular models to generate payload-specific physicochem­
ical and biological performance data, including mRNA-loaded particle 
size, PDI, encapsulation efficiency, cell viability, and transfection effi­
ciency. These data are further incorporated into predictive modeling to 
prioritize formulations for functional mRNA delivery. Finally, the top- 
ranked candidates are validated therapeutically using CFTR mRNA to 
assess disease-relevant CFTR protein expression. Overall, this stage 
guided workflow enables progressive refinement from broad empty-LNP 
screening and model-guided selection to payload-specific evaluation 
and CFTR mRNA validation.

2.2. High-throughput LNP formulation library construction and 
characterization

Four ionizable lipids (SM-102, ALC-0315, MC3, and CKK-E12) were 
selected, together with helper lipids (DSPC or DOPC), cholesterol, and 
DMG-PEG2000. The formulation design was guided by clinically vali­
dated ratios (e.g., Onpattro, Moderna) [37,38], but expanded to cover 
ionizable lipid concentrations ranging from 1.25 to 10 mM and sys­
tematically varied molar ratios (Table 1). In total, 864 distinct formu­
lations were generated.

LNPs were synthesized using the parallelized microfluidic platform 
MiNANO-form (as shown in Fig. 1). Lipids were dissolved in ethanol 
(organic phase, 100 μL) and mixed with 25 mM sodium acetate buffer 
(NaOAc, pH 5.0; aqueous phase, 300 μL) at a flow rate ratio of 3:1 and a 
total flow rate of 2000 μL/min. Based on the previous study [36], 
increasing the total flow rate above 2000 μL/min did not result in further 
changes in particle size. After microfluidic mixing, 40 μL of the LNP 
suspension was dispensed into 96-well plates prefilled with 160 μL PBS. 
Size and PDI were measured using a high-throughput DynaPro™ Plate 
Reader III (5 s per measurement, 30 acquisitions per sample). Individual 
acquisitions reporting a PDI value of 0 were excluded from analysis prior 
to calculating the final particle size and PDI values.
2.3. AI-driven optimization of empty LNP formulations

To enable systematic exploration of the formulation space, key 
formulation variables including lipid types, molar ratios, and

concentrations were expanded into a comprehensive feature set con­
sisting of formulation component molecular concentrations, formulation 
component ratios, lipid type information, and pairwise ratio features. 
The original six formulation variables did not fully capture the absolute 
concentrations and relative proportions of all four components. There­
fore, additional concentration- and ratio-derived descriptors were 
generated to provide a more complete physicochemical representation 
of each formulation. Pairwise ratio features were further included to 
explicitly encode the relative balance between lipid components, since 
normalization of individual features may reduce the representation of 
component-to-component proportional relationships. This feature- 
engineering step is used to improve physicochemical representation 
and support predictive model training.

The initial dataset comprised six primary features: ionizable lipid 
type, helper lipid type, ionizable lipid ratio (%), helper lipid ratio (%), 
PEG-lipid ratio (%), and ionizable lipid concentration (mmol/mL). 
Eleven additional engineered features were subsequently generated, 
yielding a total of 17 features grouped into four categories:

⋅ Formulation component molecular concentrations: ionizable 
lipid concentration (ILC), helper lipid concentration (HLC), PEG- 
lipid concentration (PLC), cholesterol concentration (CC), and total 
lipid concentration (TLC).
⋅ Formulation component ratios: ionizable lipid ratio (ILR), helper 
lipid ratio (HLR), PEG-lipid ratio (PLR), and cholesterol ratio (CR).
⋅ Lipid type information: ionizable lipid type (ILT) and helper lipid 
type (HLT).
⋅ Pairwise ratio features: ionizable/helper ratio (I_H_R), ionizable/ 
PEG ratio (I_P_R), ionizable/cholesterol ratio (I_C_R), helper/PEG 
ratio (H_P_R), helper/cholesterol ratio (H_C_R), and PEG/cholesterol 
ratio (P_C_R).

The prediction of size was formulated as a regression task, whereas 
PDI prediction was framed as a binary classification problem (≤0.2 vs. 
> 0.2). Candidate algorithms for size prediction included Gaussian 
Process Regression (GPR), Support Vector Regression (SVR), Random 
Forest (RF), Gradient Boosting Regression (GBR), Extreme Gradient 
Boosting Regression (XGBR), Ridge Regression (Ridge), and Artificial 
Neural Network (ANN). For PDI classification, the candidate algorithms 
were RF, Gradient Boosting (GB), Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGB), 
Gaussian Process (GP), Support Vector Machine (SVM), and Multi-Layer 
Perceptron (MLP). These algorithms were selected because the dataset is 
relatively small and the underlying relationships between LNP formu­
lation variables and physicochemical properties are likely nonlinear. 
The chosen models are well suited for small-sample settings while 
maintaining sufficient flexibility to capture complex nonlinear 
input–output mappings. Potential outliers in particle size and PDI were 
assessed separately before model development. For each formulation, 
the five nearest neighbours were identified using Euclidean distance in 
the normalized formulation-feature space, excluding the formulation 
itself. The local deviation was defined as the absolute difference between 
the observed endpoint value and the mean value of its five nearest 
neighbours. For each endpoint, formulations with local deviations 
exceeding Q3 + 0.75 × IQR of the corresponding deviation distribution, 
where Q3 is the third quartile and IQR is the interquartile range, were 
excluded from model training. A 5 × 5 nested cross-validation strategy 
with 20 repetitions was employed for robust model selection and 
hyperparameter optimization. The dataset was split into five outer folds, 
with one-fold held out for testing and the remaining four subjected to a 
five-fold inner loop for hyperparameter tuning. The best parameters 
from the inner loop were used to train a model evaluated on the outer 
test fold, and this process was repeated across all outer folds. To reduce 
variance from a single random split, the entire procedure was repeated 
20 times with different random seeds, yielding 100 outer test evalua­
tions per model and providing a robust distribution of performance 
metrics.

After selecting the best-performing model for each task, SHAP-based 
recursive feature elimination (SHAP-RFE) was applied to refine the 
input space. At each iteration, one feature was removed, the model was 
retrained, and performance was evaluated using 10-fold cross- 
validation, with hyperparameters fixed to those most frequently 
selected during nested cross-validation. Specifically, for size prediction, 
features were retained if their removal increased the cross-validated 
mean absolute error (MAE). For PDI classification, features were 
retained if removing them reduced the precision of the monodisperse 
class (PDI ≤0.2). This process produced compact feature sets that pre­
served predictive accuracy while improving interpretability.

The optimized models were applied to screen a candidate design 
space generated by systematic sampling of lipid ratios (ionizable lipid: 
40–60%, helper lipid: 4–16%, PEG-lipid: 0.5–2.5%) and total lipid 
concentrations (0.0025–0.01 mmol/mL). Formulations predicted to 
yield particle sizes below 80 nm with monodisperse PDI (≤0.2) were 
shortlisted. Sobol sequence sampling was subsequently employed to 
maximize chemical and compositional diversity within this subset.

2.5. AI-driven optimization of GFP mRNA-loaded LNPs

To integrate physicochemical characteristics with biological perfor­
mance, GFP mRNA transfection data from the 100 representative for­
mulations (selected via Sobol sampling) were incorporated into the AI 
pipeline. Following log transformation of the transfection efficiency 
values, a regression framework was established to directly predict 
transfection efficiency from formulation descriptors, following the same 
feature engineering, nested cross-validation, and SHAP-RFE in Section 
2.3. The model was developed as an exploratory tool for candidate 
prioritization within the experimentally sampled formulation space, 
rather than for resolving lipid-class-independent effects of individual 
formulation descriptors. Because transfection efficiency was treated as a 
regression endpoint, SHAP-RFE was performed using MAE as the pri­
mary performance criterion, consistent with the size-prediction task. 
Model predictions were extended to all formulations previously filtered 
by physicochemical thresholds (size <80 nm, PDI ≤0.2). The top six 
candidates, representing both DSPC- and DOPC-based formulations, 
were subsequently selected for downstream experimental validation.
2.6. CFTR mRNA encapsulation and western blot analysis

The six lead formulations were synthesized with CFTR mRNA for 
functional validation. CFBE cells were seeded in 12-well plates (60,000 
cells/well) and treated with LNPs containing 3 μg CFTR mRNA. After 48 
h, cells were lysed with RIPA buffer containing protease inhibitors. Total 
protein was quantified with a BCA assay, separated by 7% Tris-Acetate 
gels, and transferred to nitrocellulose membranes. Western blotting was 
performed using a mouse anti-human CFTR primary antibody (UNC- 
596, 1:500) and a mouse anti-GAPDH primary antibody (Abcam, 
1:2000) as the loading control. The secondary antibody used for 
detection was an HRP-conjugated anti-mouse IgG (Cell Signaling 
Technology, 1:2000). Bands were visualized using Pierce™ ECL sub­
strate and imaged with an iBright CL750 system.

The mean ± standard deviation (±SD) was presented for all data. For 
nanoparticle characterization (size and PDI), each formulation was 
measured in triplicate within a single preparation to account for tech­
nical variation. For cell-based experiments, each condition was tested in 
three wells per experiment. One-way ANOVA with Dunnett's multiple- 
comparison tests was used to analyze the difference for different 
groups using Prism 8.0 (GraphPad). A difference was considered sig­
nificant if P < 0.05 (*P < 0.05, **P < 0.01, ***P < 0.001, ****P <
0.0001). The complete source code and machine-learning workflow 
used in this study are publicly available at https://github.com/luh

3.2. Empty LNP formulation optimization based on size and PDI
3.2.1. Model selection for size and PDI prediction

Following endpoint-specific outlier removal, 824 formulations were 
included in the size regression and PDI classification analyses, respec­
tively. As shown in Fig. 3a and b, regression and classification tasks 
revealed distinct performance differences. For size prediction, GPR, 
SVR, RF, GBR, and XGBR achieved similar accuracy, with average 
percent errors around 11.5%, MSE values of 44–48, MAE values of 
5.1–5.4, and R2 values between 0.76 and 0.78, and exhibited stable 
distributions across 100 nested CV runs. Ridge and ANN performed 
worse, with higher errors and lower R [2], the latter showing highly 
scattered predictions. GPR was therefore selected as the most suitable

regressor, yielding the best R2 and lowest errors. For PDI classification, 
RF, XGB, GB, and GP consistently achieved accuracies of 0.69–0.75, F1 
scores of 0.80–0.85, and precision and recall above 0.80, with stable 
results across repetitions. In contrast, SVM was less consistent, and Lo­
gistic Regression performed poorly (accuracy below 0.3, near-zero 
precision and recall, minimal F1). RF was selected for PDI classifica­
tion because it showed high accuracy and consistent precision across 
repeated nested CV runs.

vidual formulation features (Fig. 3c and d). A total of 17 formulation

optimization.

3.2.3. Feature contribution and data scaling analysis

To evaluate whether the dataset size was sufficient to support reli­
able model training, a learning curve analysis was first performed by 
progressively increasing the training set size and assessing the predictive 
performance of the Gaussian Process Regressor (GPR) on the size 
endpoint (Fig. 4b). The test MAE decreased monotonically from 
approximately 7.65 at 40 samples to below 4.54 at 659 samples, indi­
cating improved predictive accuracy with increasing data availability. 
The most pronounced reduction in error occurred at smaller sample 
sizes, while the curve gradually plateaued beyond ~400 samples, sug­
gesting diminishing returns from further data expansion. These results 
indicate that the current dataset provides sufficient coverage to capture 
the dominant formulation–property relationships, although additional 
data may still yield incremental improvements.

To further investigate the relative contribution of different feature 
groups to model performance, a systematic feature group ablation (FGA) 
analysis was conducted. In this procedure, the GPR model was retrained 
under keep-only configurations, where only one or a combination of 
predefined feature groups were retained, together with ionizable lipid 
type (one-hot encoded) as baseline covariates. The evaluated feature 
groups included concentration-based features (Conc), composition per­
centages (Comp), and derived ratios (Der), as well as their combinations. 
Model performance was assessed using MAE, MSE, and R [2], with re­
sults expressed as relative changes compared to the full feature set.

As shown in Fig. 4a, retaining only concentration features (Conc) 
results in model performance comparable to that of the full feature set, 
with minimal changes across MAE, MSE, and R [2]. In contrast, models 
trained exclusively on composition (Comp) or derived ratio features

(Der) exhibit substantial performance degradation, with MAE increasing 
by more than twofold and MSE by over threefold, accompanied by a 
pronounced reduction in R2 (ΔR [2] ~ −0.8). Combining feature groups 
(e.g., Comp + Conc or Conc + Der) partially mitigates this degradation 
but still does not outperform the concentration-only configuration. 
These findings indicate that absolute concentration features are the 
dominant determinants of predictive performance in size modeling, 
whereas ratio-based and compositional descriptors provide limited 
additional information when used independently. This observation is 
consistent with physicochemical principles, as absolute molar concen­
trations more directly govern nanoparticle self-assembly processes than 
relative composition descriptors.

FGA and learning curve analyses were not performed for the PDI 
classifier. As shown in Fig. S3, the model exhibits limited predictive 
performance for class 0, while maintaining relatively high precision for 
class 1 (PDI ≤0.2), which represents the primary target for formulation 
optimization. This enables reliable identification of low-PDI formula­
tions, consistent with the intended application of the model. Given this 
task-oriented design and the imbalance in predictive performance be­
tween classes, further ablation or scaling analyses were not considered 
informative for the PDI model.

increased from 50 to 100 formulations. With a fixed 80/20 train-test 
split, this corresponded to training set sizes from 40 to 80 samples. 
Test MAE decreased from approximately 1.0 to ~0.90 as the training set 
size increased, with little additional improvement at larger sample sizes. 
At larger training sizes, the test MAE approached a plateau, suggesting 
diminishing improvement for the combined GPR model under the cur­
rent dataset structure.

The trained model was then used to screen formulations within the 
SM-102 design space. This focused screening step was performed 
because SM-102 formulations showed a wider range of GFP expression 
than CKK-E12 formulations in the experimental dataset, whereas CKK- 
E12 formulations had consistently low transfection signals. Candidate 
formulations were first constrained by the predefined physicochemical 
criteria used in the empty LNP screen (size <80 nm and PDI ≤0.2). 
Among the remaining SM-102 candidates, six formulations, including 
three DSPC-based and three DOPC-based formulations, were selected 
based on predicted GFP expression for experimental validation 
(Table S2).

ated for CFTR mRNA delivery in CFBE cells (formulations were shown in 
Table. S2). Their physicochemical properties are shown in Fig. 7a, b. All

Functional performance was further assessed by Western blot analysis 
(Fig. 7d). All six formulations induced detectable CFTR protein expres­

bands than their DSPC-containing counterparts. Densitometric quanti­

trend (Fig. 7c), with SM-102-DOPC-1 showing the highest CFTR 
expression among the tested LNP formulations. Although the commer­

expression, its expression level was not significantly different from that 
of the best-performing DOPC-containing formulation. These results are 
broadly consistent with the model-guided prediction that DOPC- 
containing formulations would show stronger CFTR mRNA delivery 
than DSPC-containing formulations, supporting the potential utility of 
the screening model for formulation prioritization.

In this study, we introduce ELEVATE-LNP, a stage guided platform 
for mRNA–LNP formulation optimization. As summarized in Fig. 8, 
ELEVATE-LNP organizes formulation development into three inter­
connected stages: broad physicochemical space mapping using empty 
LNPs, payload-specific functional screening using mRNA-loaded LNPs, 
and disease-relevant validation using CFTR mRNA. The platform is 
primarily intended for midstream and downstream optimization after 
promising ionizable lipids have been shortlisted, allowing lipid com­
positions and molar ratios to be systematically refined. In the first stage, 
864 empty LNP formulations containing four ionizable lipids, ALC-0315, 
SM-102, MC3, and CKK-E12, were prepared using a high-throughput 
microfluidic platform and characterized by high-throughput DLS. The 
resulting formulation-level dataset was used to train machine learning 
models for empty-LNP size and PDI prediction. These models were then 
applied to an expanded virtual formulation space comprising 211,344 
formulations across the four ionizable lipid systems, among which 
46,004 formulations met the predefined physicochemical criteria of 
particle size <80 nm and PDI ≤0.2. Because the subsequent mRNA- 
loaded screening focused on SM-102 and CKK-E12, 100,672 virtual 
formulations from these two lipid systems were further considered. 
Among them, 26,450 formulations satisfied the physicochemical

selection criteria, including 20,884 SM-102-based formulations and 
5566 CKK-E12-based formulations. To obtain an experimentally 
manageable and representative subset for payload-specific evaluation, 
100 formulations were selected from this eligible candidate pool using 
Sobol sequence-based sampling, with 50 formulations from each ioniz­
able lipid system. These formulations were then loaded with GFP mRNA 
and evaluated for particle size, PDI, encapsulation efficiency, cell 
viability, and transfection efficiency. Since SM-102-based formulations 
showed superior GFP mRNA transfection performance under the tested 
conditions, six SM-102-based candidates, including three DSPC- 
containing and three DOPC-containing formulations, were further 
selected for CFTR mRNA loading and Western blot validation.

The predicted formulation landscapes further illustrate the 
complexity of LNP formulation design. Across the four ionizable lipid 
systems, particle size and PDI exhibited nonlinear and lipid-dependent 
responses to variations in formulation composition, as shown in 
Fig. 9a and b. These findings suggest that LNP assembly may not be 
adequately described using conventional one-factor-at-a-time optimi­
zation, because comparable changes in lipid ratio or total lipid con­
centration can produce distinct physicochemical outcomes depending 
on the chemistry of the ionizable lipid. Consequently, for­
mulation–property relationships identified for one lipid system may not 
be directly transferable to another. In this context, the ELEVATE-LNP 
microfluidics–machine learning framework provides a practical 
approach for mapping multidimensional formulation spaces and 
excluding candidates with unfavorable particle size or PDI before 
resource-intensive mRNA encapsulation and biological evaluation. 
Following mRNA loading, the particle-size distribution generally shifted 
toward larger values compared with the corresponding empty LNPs 
(Fig. 9c). The increase in particle size, defined as ΔS, ranged from 
approximately 0 to 120 nm, with a mean increase of approximately 50 
nm, while most formulations exhibited increases below approximately 
70 nm (Fig. 9d). These results provide an empirical reference for 
defining initial empty-LNP size thresholds during prescreening. Never­
theless, because the magnitude of the size increase remained 
formulation-dependent, ΔS should be regarded as a preliminary 
screening guide rather than a direct prediction rule. Experimental 
characterization of mRNA-loaded LNPs therefore remains essential for 
payload-specific formulation optimization.

The ELEVATE-LNP framework is particularly suited to midstream 
and downstream LNP optimization after promising ionizable lipids have

been shortlisted. During early-stage ionizable lipid development, a 
small-scale preliminary transfection assay may first be used to identify 
lipid classes with sufficient biological activity in the target cell type, 
while candidates with minimal transfection potential can be excluded 
before entering a larger formulation-screening workflow. For shortlisted 
ionizable lipids, ELEVATE-LNP can then be applied to systematically 
refine lipid composition, molar ratios, and formulation conditions. 
Empty-LNP screening first identifies regions of the formulation space 
with suitable particle size and PDI, after which mRNA encapsulation and 
functional evaluation are performed on a more focused candidate set. By 
concentrating experimental resources on preselected ionizable lipid 
systems, this staged approach can reduce mRNA consumption, limit the 
number of cell-based assays required, and improve the efficiency of lead 
formulation identification.

Several limitations should be addressed in future work. First, 
although the current study included four ionizable lipids in the empty- 
LNP library, the mRNA-loaded functional screening was focused on 
SM-102 and CKK-E12. Because SM-102-based formulations showed 
higher and more variable GFP expression, whereas CKK-E12-based for­
mulations exhibited limited transfection performance under the tested 
conditions, the combined model may partly reflect lipid-class-associated

differences. This dataset structure limits the ability to distinguish lipid- 
class effects from continuous formulation effects within each class and 
therefore constrains the mechanistic interpretation of the SHAP-RFE 
results. Larger lipid-specific datasets with broader within-class 
response distributions, together with evaluation of mRNA-loaded for­
mulations containing additional ionizable lipids such as ALC-0315 and 
MC3, will be needed to resolve these effects and improve the general­
izability of the workflow. Second, the present biological evaluation was 
performed mainly in vitro using CFBE cells. Future studies should 
include more physiologically relevant airway models and in vivo vali­
dation to assess biodistribution, tissue-specific delivery, safety, and 
therapeutic relevance. Disease-relevant models such as CF mouse 
models or reporter ferret models could provide important platforms for 
evaluating pulmonary mRNA delivery and CFTR expression. Finally, 
integration with automated formulation preparation and high- 
throughput microfluidic production systems will further improve the 
scalability and reproducibility of this workflow by reducing manual 
handling, operator-dependent variability, and experimental error.

In conclusion, this study presents ELEVATE-LNP, a stage guided 
framework for midstream and downstream mRNA–LNP formulation 
optimization. Empty-LNP characterization is used as an initial physi­
cochemical filtering step, rather than as a substitute for direct evaluation 
of mRNA-loaded LNPs. By integrating high-throughput microfluidic 
screening, AI-guided candidate down-selection, ELEVATE-LNP enables 
broad exploration of formulation design spaces while significantly 
reducing the experimental burden associated with mRNA encapsulation 
and cell-based testing. In the disease-relevant CFTR mRNA validation 
stage, the six selected formulations showed particle sizes below 160 nm 
and PDI values below 0.2. Western blot analysis further showed 
detectable CFTR protein expression for the selected formulations, and 
several formulations achieved expression levels that were not statisti­
cally different from Lipofectamine MessengerMAX under the tested 
conditions. Overall, ELEVATE-LNP provides a practical midstream and 
downstream optimization strategy for refining lipid compositions, 
formulation ratios, and process conditions within shortlisted ionizable 
lipid systems. Further validation using newly developed ionizable lipids, 
automated workflows, and advanced airway models will be required to 
assess its broader scalability and translational relevance.

issues.review_question: 确认汇总统计属性；不把三次测量当作三个独立制备批次。

issues.source: main.pdf section 2.3; si2/si3 column D; SI Table S1
issues.issue: Concentration units vary between mM and mmol/mL in different locations.
issues.handling: Keep Excel mM; do not transfer SI Table S1 numeric concentrations without checking units.
issues.review_question: 审核浓度单位及其所指相：混合前还是混合后。

issues.issue: Only four rows contain numeric actual empty size; other rows use a dash.
issues.handling: Record missing_marker, not zero and not paper-wide not_reported.
issues.review_question: 缺失符号仅反映该单元格，是否能在其他来源补齐需另外取证。

issues.issue: Table S1 numbers have not been matched to individual Fig.7 bar labels.
issues.handling: Register four result slots per candidate as unresolved visual extraction; no numeric assignment.

issues.issue: Methods list Olympus CKX41 in equipment and Olympus IX81 for GFP imaging.
issues.handling: Use endpoint-specific raw wording; retain discrepancy for review.

issues.issue: CFTR size described as below 150 nm in results and below 160 nm in conclusion.
issues.handling: Keep both as group-level statements; do not turn bounds into exact per-formulation results.

issues.issue: Delta size is loaded measured size minus predicted empty size.
issues.handling: Do not describe it as two paired measured sizes or create an empty-to-loaded experimental match.

issues.source: si1.docx Table S1 HLP and ILC headers
issues.issue: HLP differs from HLR notation; ILC unit not specified in table.
issues.handling: Keep raw headers, no automatic unit conversion or label replacement.

issues.issue: Positive control has no equivalent LNP composition row.
issues.handling: Register control separately; no invented formulation or exact plotted value.
